The chart displays the English words for the primes and some of their combinatorial possibilities, according to NSM grammar.\\nMore complex combinations are also possible. In some languages, two primes e.g. feel and hear may be expressed by the same word. In some languages, a prime can have two or more\\nexponents (allolexes), e.g. English other and else. Sometimes a combination of two or more primes, e.g. like this, can be expressed by a single portmanteau word. [hello@nsm-approach.net].\\nFor more resources visit https://nsm-approach.net\\nUsing NSM in explications\\nDon\u2019t include any complex English-specific words,\\nno matter how common and seemingly basic, e.g.\\nand, or, make.\\nEnsure that you use semantic primes only in\\nallowable syntactic frames. Do not resort to non-\\nNSM syntax even if English grammar allows it. For\\nexample, avoid \u2018do something about it\u2019 and \u2018feel\\ngood/bad about something\u2019; semantic primes DO\\nand FEEL do not have any \u201cabout\u201d valency.\\nAvoid the following non-universal constructions:\\n- relative clauses (e.g. someone who did this)\\n- comparative (e.g. better than, more than)\\n- indirect speech (e.g. this someone said that ...)\\nWhenever possible, explications should be written\\nentirely in semantic primes but some explications\\nrequire use of semantic molecules in addition to\\nprimes. Semantic molecules are a well-defined set\\nof non-primitive meanings that function as units in\\nthe meanings of more complex concepts.\\nFunction words and portmanteaus\\nThese are some of the main function words and\\nportmanteau expressions in English-based NSM.\\n\u2018in\u2019, e.g. in this place; in one moment\\n\u2018at\u2019, e.g. at this time; at this moment\\n\u2018of\u2019, e.g. one of these people; something of one kind\\n\u2018with\u2019, e.g. do something with someone/something\\n\u2018about\u2019, e.g. think/say about something/someone\\n\u2018these\u2019: variant of \u2018this\u2019 used with a plural noun\\n\u2018it\u2019 (dummy subject), e.g. it is good if ..., it is bad if...\\n\u2018it\u2019 for \u2018this thing\u2019\\n\u2018a lot\u2019: a variant of \u2018very much~many\u2019\\n\u2018well\u2019: an adverbial variant of \u2018good\u2019\\n\u2018such\u2019: portmanteau of \u2018like\u2019 and \u2018this\u2019\\n\u2018they\u2019 or \u2018them\u2019 for \u2018these people\u2019 or \u2018these things\u2019\\n\u2018everywhere\u2019: portmanteau based on \u2018all\u2019 and \u2018place\u2019\\n\u2018often\u2019, \u2018sometimes\u2019, \u2018always\u2019, \u2018never\u2019: portmanteaus\\nbased on quantifiers and \u2018time\u2019\\nsingular \u2018they\u2019 for \u2018this someone\u2019 (if you want to use\\nthis portmanteau, please note it in the text)\\f\", \"definition\": \"NSM v20 lexical unit GOOD.
